_doc.what_this_is: A WORKED, schema-valid example of verify/verify_map.json for a neutral toy topic ('city transit ridership', matching reproducible_notebook.md). COPY THE STRUCTURE, REPLACE THE CONTENT: it carries one entry of each of the four real kinds (computation [exact + montecarlo], media, generated, fact). On YOUR blog, author one entry per data-* id that actually appears in index.html (data-ana / data-det / data-des / data-sct / data-cin / data-int). Delete every entry whose kind your page does not use; never ship this transit content verbatim.
_doc.purpose: verify_map.json is the per-element provenance map the Inspector panel reads. Each non-underscore key is an ATOMIC element id that also appears as a data-* attribute in index.html. Clicking that element opens the Inspector drawer, which renders this entry.
_doc.kind_selects_renderer: The `kind` field selects which drawer renderer is used: 'computation' -> code + data_preview + expected_output + run panel (optionally a client-side reduced-N rerun); 'media' -> asset preview + source_url + license + identity provenance; 'generated' -> AI-asset preview + tool/model/prompt/disclosure + the real_default fallback; 'fact' -> claim + categorised sources[] with per-source facts[]; 'credits' -> the same fact renderer with a 'Credits' badge (a license/source aggregator).
_doc.numbers_are_real: Every expected_output below was produced by running the matching run_cells.example.json snippet with python and pasting the actual stdout. Never invent these — a wrong example teaches the wrong habit.
_doc.byte_identity: verify_map.json must be byte-identical to the inline `verifyMap` <script> island embedded in index.html. The Inspector reads the inline copy at runtime; this file is the on-disk source of truth and the auditable artifact.

ana_crowd_risk.title: Red line crowding risk — about one weekday in six runs over capacity
ana_crowd_risk.claim: On a typical weekday the Red line carries 182,400 boardings, but day-to-day demand swings enough that it exceeds its 195,000 comfortable-capacity threshold on roughly 18% of weekdays — about one day in six. That is the share of 200,000 simulated weekdays in which boardings cross the line, not a forecast for any single day.
ana_crowd_risk.code:
# build_crowding.py — chance the Red line exceeds its 195k crowding threshold.
# Daily boardings ~ Normal(mean=182.4k, sd=14.0k), fit on ridership.csv.
import numpy as np
MEAN_K, SD_K, THRESHOLD_K = 182.4, 14.0, 195.0
N, SEED = 200000, 4326
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
daily = rng.normal(MEAN_K, SD_K, N)
p_over = (daily > THRESHOLD_K).mean()
print(f"Red line crowding risk (published Monte-Carlo, N={N:,}, seed={SEED})")
print(f"  P(weekday boardings > {THRESHOLD_K:.0f}k) = {p_over*100:.1f}%")

data_preview.description: The mean/spread of weekday Red-line boardings fit from ridership.csv (the distribution the simulation samples).

ana_crowd_risk.expected_output:
Red line crowding risk (published Monte-Carlo, N=200,000, seed=4326)

run.note: In-browser the Inspector runs a reduced N=10,000 sample, graded '≈ within noise' against the published 18.4% (full N=200,000), never a hard PASS.

ana_line_share.title: The Red line alone is over a third of the network
ana_line_share.claim: Average weekday boardings are heavily concentrated on the busiest line: the Red line carries 182,400 weekday boardings, 35.8% of the 509,000-boarding network, more than the Gold and Silver lines combined. The five lines split the network 35.8 / 25.7 / 19.0 / 11.4 / 8.0, a steep ladder rather than an even spread.
ana_line_share.code:
import pandas as pd
# Inlined from ridership.csv: average weekday boardings per line (thousands).
df = pd.DataFrame(
    [["Red", 182.4], ["Blue", 131.0], ["Green", 96.6],
     ["Gold", 58.2], ["Silver", 40.8]],
    columns=["line", "weekday_boardings_k"])
total = df["weekday_boardings_k"].sum()
df["share_pct"] = (df["weekday_boardings_k"] / total * 100).round(1)
df = df.sort_values("weekday_boardings_k", ascending=False)
for _, r in df.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r.line:7} {r.weekday_boardings_k:6.1f}k  {r.share_pct:5.1f}%")

data_preview.description: Average weekday boardings (thousands) and each line's share of the network (ridership.csv).

det_history.title: A century-old network still carrying half a million a day
det_history.claim: The Red line opened in 1912 and is the oldest of the five routes in the network, which together carry on the order of half a million weekday boardings. Ridership fell sharply during the 2020 pandemic and has recovered toward — but not fully back to — its pre-pandemic weekday level, which is the backdrop against which the per-line crowding figures should be read.
